questions.q: A model scores 100% on training data but 85% on held-out data. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: A big drop from training to held-out performance is the classic sign of overfitting (high variance).

questions.q: A model scores about 80% on both training and held-out data, and you know a better model can reach 90%. What is going on?
options: Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the pattern
questions.explain: Poor performance on the training set itself means the model lacks capacity. That is high bias, or underfitting.

questions.q: Why can't you choose a model's flexibility (such as tree depth) by looking only at training accuracy?
options: Training accuracy is not computable for trees
Training accuracy keeps rising as flexibility rises, so it always favors the most overfit model
questions.explain: More flexibility always fits the training rows better. Only held-out data reveals when extra flexibility starts to hurt.

questions.q: Which is an appropriate response to OVERFITTING?
options: Constrain the model, for example by limiting tree depth, or use regularization
Train for longer on the same rows with no changes
questions.explain: Overfitting is too much flexibility. Constrain the model, simplify it, add data, or use ensembling.

questions.q: You chose the best max_depth by picking the highest held-out accuracy across 15 candidates. What is the concern?
options: None: this gives a perfectly unbiased estimate
Held-out accuracy can never be used for selection
The chosen score is slightly optimistic, so a separate untouched test set is needed for the final estimate
Depth should always be chosen randomly
questions.explain: Selecting the winner on the same rows you score it on inflates the estimate. A three-way split with a validation set and an untouched test set fixes this.
